item.title: Grafana Alerting vs Alertmanager: rules, routing and coexistence
item.description: Compare Grafana Alerting with Prometheus and Alertmanager: rule ownership, data sources, notification routing, coexistence and a practical way to choose.
item.content:encoded:
Choose Prometheus with Alertmanager when your rules belong with your metrics and are maintained as code. Choose Grafana-managed alerting when you need Grafana to evaluate queries across supported data sources and manage conditions through its UI or provisioning tools. You can also keep Prometheus rules, add Grafana-managed rules for other data, and use the same external Alertmanager for notification delivery.

The important decision is where a rule runs and who owns its notifications. Here is how to make those choices without evaluating the same condition twice.

What you are comparing​

Prometheus evaluates PromQL alerting rules. When an expression produces a matching label set, Prometheus tracks that alert's state and, once its pending period has elapsed, sends a firing alert downstream. Alertmanager handles the delivery side: deduplication, grouping, routing, silences and inhibition. It does not query your metrics or evaluate the PromQL threshold. See the official alerting rules and Alertmanager overview.

Grafana Alerting includes a rule evaluator and notification management. With a Grafana-managed rule, Grafana executes the queries, evaluates the condition and produces alert instances. Its notification configuration then decides where those alerts go. The data source must support backend alerting; a query that works on a dashboard is not sufficient proof. Grafana documents that requirement here.

Two common paths therefore look like this:

Prometheus evaluates rules → Prometheus Alertmanager → receivers

Grafana evaluates rules    → Grafana's Alertmanager   → contact points

The storage system can be the same Prometheus in both cases. Moving evaluation to Grafana does not require moving the stored metrics.

Grafana Alerting vs Prometheus + Alertmanager​

DecisionPrometheus + AlertmanagerGrafana-managed alerting
Who evaluates the condition?PrometheusGrafana
What can the rule query?Data accessible through PromQLSupported backend data sources; rules can combine queries and expressions
Where is the rule maintained?Prometheus rule files; commonly generated or deployed through GitOpsGrafana UI, provisioning files, Terraform or APIs
Who handles delivery?External AlertmanagerGrafana's notification system, or a configured external Alertmanager
How are destinations selected?Alertmanager routes and receiversContact points and notification policies, or the external Alertmanager's configuration
Can dashboards stay in Grafana?YesYes
Who diagnoses an evaluation failure?The team operating Prometheus and its rule configurationThe team operating Grafana alert evaluation and its data source access

Both designs can be managed as code. Grafana's UI is a useful option, and its provisioning tools also support reviewable configuration. Decide who is allowed to edit provisioned resources and how those edits are deployed before treating either UI as the source of truth.

Three setups that are easy to confuse​

1. Grafana displays alerts that another system evaluates​

With a data source-managed rule, a compatible external system stores and evaluates the rule. Grafana provides an interface to it. Grafana's documentation describes this separately from Grafana-managed rules.

Check which API the data source exposes. A Mimir or Loki ruler, a plain Prometheus server and an Alertmanager do different jobs. Adding an Alertmanager data source does not give Grafana a general-purpose API for editing Prometheus rule files.

2. Grafana evaluates rules and uses its own notifications​

Grafana owns both the evaluation and the delivery configuration. This fits a team that already operates Grafana, needs conditions over multiple supported sources, and wants one place to maintain those rules.

For each data source, verify the evaluator's credentials and network access. A dashboard viewed by a logged-in person and a background alert evaluation can have different access conditions.

3. Grafana evaluates rules and sends them to an external Alertmanager​

This is a useful coexistence model:

Prometheus rules ─┐
                 ├→ external Alertmanager → existing receivers
Grafana rules ────┘

It lets a team keep its established routes and receivers while adding Grafana-managed evaluation. Grafana documents two ways to configure this: forward all Grafana-managed alerts to an enabled Alertmanager, or use an Alertmanager contact point for selected alerts. Adding the data source alone does not enable forwarding.

Keep the route labels consistent. For example, both evaluators might attach team="payments" and env="prod", so an existing payments route can match either source. The alert names should still describe the conditions distinctly.

A small example: who detects the outage?​

Here is a Prometheus rule that checks whether a scraped target has been unreachable for five minutes:

groups:
  - name: service-availability
    rules:
      - alert: ServiceTargetDown
        expr: up{job="checkout"} == 0
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: warning
          team: payments
        annotations:
          summary: "Checkout target is unreachable"

Prometheus evaluates up, owns the five-minute pending state and sends the alert with the team label. Alertmanager can then route it to the payments receiver.

If you recreate the condition as a Grafana-managed rule, Grafana becomes a second evaluator. That may be appropriate during a controlled comparison, but leaving both enabled creates two independent alert identities. Sharing a destination does not guarantee they will deduplicate.

Also distinguish zero from missing. This expression matches a target whose up value is zero. It does not match a target that has disappeared from discovery and no longer has a current series. Test that case separately. Grafana-managed rules also have explicit No Data and Error handling, which should be reviewed when translating a rule.

Can Grafana edit Alertmanager routes?​

The answer depends on the Alertmanager implementation. For a Prometheus Alertmanager, Grafana can manage silences, but contact points, notification policies and templates are read-only in that integration: its HTTP API does not support updating those resources. Edit and deploy the external configuration through the system that owns it. Grafana calls out this limitation.

This matters when the original requirement is simply “give us a UI.” Viewing an alert, adding a silence, editing a routing tree and authoring a detection rule are four separate capabilities. Check which one your team needs before changing the architecture.

How to choose​

  • Keep Prometheus evaluation when the rules already live alongside instrumentation, changes go through code review, and PromQL covers the detection requirements. Use Grafana for dashboards and Alertmanager for delivery.
  • Choose Grafana-managed evaluation when a team needs its query and expression workflow over supported data sources, and is prepared to operate Grafana as an alerting dependency.
  • Use both with an external Alertmanager when evaluation belongs in different systems but notification ownership should remain centralized. Document which system evaluates each condition.

Start a migration with one non-critical rule. Compare its labels, firing time, recovery behavior and destination against the existing rule. Include an empty result and a failed query in the check. Then disable the old evaluator for that condition and verify that only the intended notification path remains.

High availability needs a separate review. A working dashboard does not demonstrate that evaluation and delivery will survive a failed instance. Our Prometheus HA guide separates storage redundancy from alerting redundancy.

Where Nightingale fits​

Nightingale is another evaluation option when rules need business-group ownership and a UI across metrics, logs and SQL sources. Its Grafana Alerting comparison and Prometheus + Alertmanager comparison describe the relevant trade-offs. For a database example, see SQL query alerting on failed MySQL orders.

For the wider choice, the open-source alerting platform guide separates rule evaluators, aggregation layers and on-call tools. Choose the layer that solves the operational requirement first.

item.title: SQL query alerting: monitor failed orders in MySQL
item.description: Build a MySQL query alert for failed orders with Nightingale: a bounded SQL window, numeric result fields, stable labels, recovery behavior and query-cost checks.
item.content:encoded:
SQL query alerting runs a query on a schedule and checks a numeric result against a condition. It is useful when the number you care about already lives in a business database: failed orders, overdue jobs or a queue that has stopped draining.

This example counts failed orders in MySQL over the last five minutes and configures Nightingale to alert when that count stays at five or more for two minutes. It also handles the quiet case: no failed orders should produce a numeric zero that lets the alert recover.

Decide what a failed order means​

For this example, an application writes one final outcome per order into order_outcomes. The row is immutable after completion. completed_at is a UTC DATETIME(6), and status is either paid or failed.

Here is a minimal schema for a scratch database:

CREATE TABLE order_outcomes (
    order_id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    channel VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL,
    completed_at DATETIME(6) NOT NULL,
    INDEX alert_window (completed_at, status, channel)
);

If your application records individual payment attempts, counting rows would count attempts rather than orders. If it updates the same order from failed to paid after a retry, the result measures current state rather than historical failures. Choose the table and timestamp that match the question you want the alert to answer.

The explicit UTC convention matters. MySQL DATETIME does not perform the session time-zone conversion that TIMESTAMP does. This example therefore compares it with UTC_TIMESTAMP(6). Adapt both sides together if your application uses a different convention. MySQL explains the type behavior here.

Write a query that also represents zero​

SELECT COUNT(*) AS failed_orders
FROM order_outcomes
WHERE status = 'failed'
  AND completed_at >= UTC_TIMESTAMP(6) - INTERVAL 5 MINUTE
  AND completed_at < UTC_TIMESTAMP(6);

The lower bound keeps the scan within the recent window. The upper bound excludes future-dated rows. MySQL's current-time functions are evaluated consistently within a statement, so the two boundaries describe one window. See the date and time function reference.

Most importantly, COUNT(*) without GROUP BY returns one row even when nothing matches:

failed_orders
0

That is a successful observation of zero failures. A query error or an absent result is a different condition. MySQL documents the empty-input behavior of COUNT here.

Connect the database and map the result​

In Nightingale, register a MySQL data source with an account that has SELECT access to the required table. Set its associated alerting engine cluster, connection limits and timeout. The SQL database setup guide covers those fields.

Create a MySQL alert rule, select that data source, and put the statement above in query A. Under Auxiliary settings, set:

SettingValue
Value fieldfailed_orders
Label fieldEmpty: this query returns only the numeric column
Trigger expression$A.failed_orders >= 5
Execution frequency@every 60s as a starting point
For duration120 seconds
Recovery configurationRecover only when data exists and the trigger condition is not met

The threshold and schedule are example settings, not recommended limits for every service. With a 60-second schedule and a 120-second pending period, detection requires several consecutive matching evaluations. It is not an exact timer starting at the fifth failed order. The evaluation and recovery guide explains the timing.

Use Preview on the rule's query card to check the value. In Nightingale's open-source edition, this MySQL workflow is in the rule form rather than the metrics explorer. Then use Test fire to check the expression and inspect evaluation records after saving.

Write the time predicate into the SQL itself. Nightingale's MySQL alert query does not supply Grafana-style $__timeFilter macros with an evaluation time range. Changing a preview time picker is not a substitute for the two bounds in this statement. The complete field mapping is in SQL-backed rules.

Add channels without losing recovery rows​

Suppose the payments team wants separate alerts for card and bank_transfer. A simple GROUP BY channel over failed rows stops returning a channel as soon as its failure count reaches zero. Under a data-required recovery policy, that missing row does not prove the alert has recovered.

Return the expected channel set and join the failures onto it:

SELECT channels.channel,
       COUNT(outcomes.order_id) AS failed_orders
FROM (
    SELECT 'card' AS channel
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'bank_transfer' AS channel
) AS channels
LEFT JOIN order_outcomes AS outcomes
  ON outcomes.channel = channels.channel
 AND outcomes.status = 'failed'
 AND outcomes.completed_at >= UTC_TIMESTAMP(6) - INTERVAL 5 MINUTE
 AND outcomes.completed_at < UTC_TIMESTAMP(6)
GROUP BY channels.channel;

The predicates stay in the ON clause, so a channel with no matches remains in the result. Count outcomes.order_id, not COUNT(*): the latter would count the unmatched left-join row as one.

Now set Value field to failed_orders and Label field to channel. Each channel becomes a separate series with a stable identity. In an application with a canonical channels table, use that instead of the two literal rows. Keep the expected set complete so new channels are not silently excluded.

Avoid order IDs, error text and timestamps as labels. They change on every evaluation or produce a series per order, while the operational question here is a count per channel.

What recovery says about the business​

When the query returns a count below five, the trigger condition no longer holds. With the recovery policy above and no additional recovery delay, the alert can recover on that successful evaluation.

This means fewer than five failures remain in the rolling five-minute window. It does not prove the underlying problem has been fixed. Old failures eventually age out even if no new orders arrive. If a broken checkout stops producing outcomes entirely, this particular count will also fall to zero. Monitor stalled processing or outcome freshness separately when that failure mode matters.

Likewise, a database connection failure must not be interpreted as a zero. Keeping an existing incident open when its result is unavailable helps, but it does not by itself create a new incident for every query failure. Monitor the query's execution status and the alerting system's health too.

Check the cost of repeated queries​

The example index begins with completed_at, allowing MySQL to consider a range over recent outcomes. Check the actual plan using EXPLAIN and measure it against representative data. An index that works on a small scratch table may not be the best one for your production distribution.

Three details matter when the query runs continuously:

  • A one-row result can still scan millions of rows. The data source's output row limit does not cap the work of COUNT(*).
  • The evaluator repeats the cost. Budget for the number of rules, data sources and evaluation cycles, and inspect the actual evaluation duration.
  • A reporting replica can be stale. If you query a replica, account for replication lag and choose a detection window that matches the freshness you can observe.

If a bounded query is still expensive, aggregate outcomes into a small reporting table or export a counter through your metrics pipeline. The symptom-based alerting guide helps choose which business failure deserves a page.

Check firing, recovery and delivery separately​

Before enabling the rule for a production team, use a scratch data source to verify these cases:

InputExpected result
No recent failuresGlobal query returns 0; channel query returns a zero for each expected channel
Five or more recent failuresCount crosses the threshold; an event appears after the configured pending period
Only old or future-dated failuresExcluded from this window
One channel becomes healthyIts row remains present with a below-threshold count
Connection or SQL errorVisible as an execution failure, not a healthy zero

Finally attach a notification rule with the appropriate severity and destination. A successful query, a firing event and a received notification are three separate checks. Use Test fire for evaluation and the notification rule's own test for delivery.

If you are choosing where to run these rules, Grafana Alerting vs Alertmanager explains evaluation and notification ownership. Nightingale's SQL rule guide covers multiple value columns, joins and the other SQL-backed data sources.

item.title: How long should a Prometheus alert wait? Data from 692 rules
item.description: We counted the for duration and severity of 692 alert rule templates. 44% use the 60s default. Here is when for: 0, 60s, 15m and 1h are the right choice.
item.content:encoded:
Every alert rule answers two questions: what counts as bad, and how long it has to stay bad. Most review effort goes into the first one, the expression and the threshold. The second is the for duration, and it often gets whatever value the tool filled in.

We wanted to know how often that happens, so we counted. Nightingale ships alert rule templates for 49 integrations. 692 rules, and 304 of them (44%) have a for duration of exactly 60 seconds, which is the default in Nightingale's rule editor. This post walks through what the numbers show and what for value suits which kind of alert.

What for does​

An alert rule is evaluated on a schedule. When the expression first returns a series, the alert is pending. It becomes firing only once the same series has kept matching on every evaluation for at least the for duration. If the series disappears for even one evaluation, the clock starts over.

Three consequences follow:

  • Detection time is about for plus one evaluation interval. A rule with for: 5m evaluated every minute fires five to six minutes after the problem starts.
  • A series that flaps never fires. If the condition comes and goes faster than for, no alert is created, and no recovery either. That is the point of for, and also a risk.
  • The defaults differ by tool. In Prometheus, leaving out for means 0, so the alert fires on the first evaluation that matches. In Nightingale's rule editor, a new rule starts at a 60-second for and a 60-second evaluation interval. The bundled templates set their own interval, almost always 15 or 30 seconds.

How we counted​

The data is the alert rule templates bundled with Nightingale's integrations: Kubernetes, Linux, MySQL, Redis, Elasticsearch and 44 more. They are published in the alert rule library and on each integration page.

  • 705 rules in total, 692 after removing exact duplicates (same integration, same name, same expression).
  • Some checks exist twice on purpose, once for Categraf metrics and once for a Prometheus exporter, because the metric names differ. We count those separately.
  • These are templates, not production configs. They show what template authors chose. They say nothing about what users changed after importing them.
  • Counted on 2026-11-01, after the two changes described in Finding 4.

The distribution​

forRulesShare
0517.4%
60s30443.9%
2m598.5%
3m679.7%
5m8612.4%
10m385.5%
15m588.4%
Over 15m263.8%

Three rules use 15s or 90s and are left out of the table.

Finding 1: the default wins, unless someone chose deliberately​

The 60-second spike is the obvious feature. We can't tell from the data whether 304 authors thought about it and picked 60s, or simply kept what the form offered. What we can see is a clear difference between where the rules came from:

  • 86 rules in the Kubernetes template keep the standard alert names from kubernetes-mixin and the Prometheus monitoring mixins, the community rule sets behind most Kubernetes monitoring stacks. 46 of them use 15 minutes, and only 2 use 60 seconds. The mixin authors set for alert by alert.
  • Rules written for Categraf and for Prometheus exporters have a median of 60 seconds. Only 4 of the 352 use 15 minutes.

Neither is wrong as a whole. The point is that a default is a choice someone else made for you, before they knew what the rule would watch. With the templates' 15- or 30-second evaluation intervals, a 60-second for means "matched on two to four evaluations in a row". That is reasonable for CPU, memory and latency. It is too short for things that recover on their own, and too long for events that are over in seconds.

Finding 2: for: 0 is right for events, if the window is wide enough​

51 rules fire on the first match (four of them are host heartbeat checks with no PromQL). Most of the rest watch something that has already happened, so waiting adds nothing:

  • A counter went up: increase(node_vmstat_oom_kill[1m]) > 0. The OOM kill happened; it will not un-happen in five minutes.
  • A deadline is close: kubelet_certificate_manager_client_ttl_seconds < 604800. Under seven days is under seven days.
  • A process restarted: mysql_global_status_uptime < 60.

The restart check hides a trap. uptime < 60 is only true for the first 60 seconds after a restart. Any for of 60 seconds or more means the alert can never fire, because uptime passes 60 before the duration is met. And the window has to fit several evaluations: copy uptime < 60 into a rule evaluated every 60 seconds, and it gets one chance per restart, which scrape delay can easily push out of the window.

The templates get this right in different ways. The MySQL and MongoDB rules use uptime < 60 with for: 0, and they evaluate every 15 seconds, so each restart gets about four chances. The Redis rules widen the window to uptime_in_seconds < 600. The Apache, EMQX and OpenLDAP rules use uptime < 300 with for: 60s. Make the window several evaluation intervals wide, keep for well under it, and keep both in mind if you change the evaluation interval.

Finding 3: some rules move the waiting into the expression​

Of the 47 for: 0 rules that have a PromQL expression, 22 wrap their metric in a range function, so the persistence check happens inside PromQL:

# GitLab's ServiceDown template, for: 0
avg_over_time(up[5m]) * 100 < 50

This is not the same as up == 0 with for: 5m:

up == 0 with for: 5mavg_over_time(up[5m]) < 0.5 with for: 0
Fires whenEvery evaluation in the last 5 minutes saw the target downThe target was down for more than half of the last 5 minutes
One good scrape in the middleResets the clockBarely moves the average
Good for"Continuously broken""Mostly broken", for flapping targets

Pick the one that matches what you mean. A target that answers one scrape in four is broken, and only the second form will say so.

Finding 4: a few instant checks deserved a longer wait​

Counting also turned up for: 0 rules that compare a sampled value against a threshold with no window at all. Two of them we changed while writing this post:

  • elasticsearch_cluster_health_status{color="yellow"} == 1. A cluster goes yellow on every rolling restart while replicas are reallocated. It now waits 10 minutes.
  • (node_nf_conntrack_entries / node_nf_conntrack_entries_limit) > 0.75. A single busy scrape was enough to trigger it. It now waits 5 minutes, the same as the sibling rule at 80%.

The tables in this post already include both changes. The general rule: give sampled gauges a few evaluation intervals, or a range function as in Finding 3. Keep for: 0 for the checks that really are binary: mysql_up == 0, a failed systemd unit, a replication thread that stopped.

Finding 5: long waits are for slow problems​

26 rules wait longer than 15 minutes. Most of them watch something that develops slowly:

  • The node filesystem predictions from kubernetes-mixin use one hour. A predict_linear forecast swings a lot on short windows; an hour of consistent prediction means the trend is real.
  • Prometheus TSDB compaction failures wait four hours. One failed compaction is noise; a run of them is a problem.
  • A kernel version mismatch across nodes waits six hours. It is a hygiene check, not an incident.
  • The slow windows of the Kubernetes API error budget burn alerts wait one and three hours. They are designed to catch slow, steady burns.

Long for values pair naturally with a lower severity. Nobody should be paged at 3 a.m. for something that took six hours to become true.

The severity side​

The same templates carry a severity. Nightingale has three levels: S1 (critical), S2 (warning) and S3 (info).

SeverityRulesShare
S2 / warning49071%
S1 / critical13720%
S3 / info609%

Five rules have no rule-level severity. When seven rules in ten share a level, the level stops helping anyone route or prioritize. A workable split:

  • S1: someone must act now. Users are affected or data is about to be lost.
  • S2: someone should look today. Capacity trends, single replicas down with redundancy left.
  • S3: record it, don't notify. Useful context during an incident.

24 templates put several severities on one rule. The Linux CPU rule, for example, uses cpu_usage_active > 75 as S3, > 85 as S2 and > 95 as S1. One rule with three tiers keeps the thresholds side by side, which is easier to review than three separate rules that drift apart.

Rules of thumb​

What the rule watchesforExample
Something that already happened0OOM kill counter increased, certificate under 7 days
A binary up/down state0 to 1 evaluation intervalmysql_up == 0
A sampled gauge: CPU, memory, latency, error rate2–3 evaluation intervalsCPU over 90%
Something that often recovers by itselfLonger than its normal recovery timeA queue that usually drains in 5 minutes: 10m
A slow trend30m to several hours, lower severityDisk full within 24 hours

for only controls when an alert starts. If an alert fires and recovers over and over, for is not the fix. Use a recovery delay instead: keep_firing_for in Prometheus, or the recover duration in Nightingale. See Evaluation interval and recovery.

Where to look next​

Every rule in the alert rule library shows its severity and its for value ("Fires after"), and links to a runbook. You can download a whole rule set as a Prometheus rules file, or import it into Nightingale from the matching integration.

item.title: kube-state-metrics vs metrics-server: which should you use?
item.description: Compare kube-state-metrics and metrics-server, then see where cAdvisor and node_exporter fit for autoscaling, resource monitoring and Kubernetes alerts.
item.content:encoded:
kube-state-metrics exposes Kubernetes object state for monitoring; metrics-server supplies recent CPU and memory usage through the Metrics API for autoscaling and kubectl top. A Deployment's missing replicas and a Pod's current CPU usage are different questions. A cluster that needs both autoscaling and object-state alerts will commonly use both components.

For a full monitoring setup, add the other two sources: cAdvisor for container resource usage and node_exporter for the host underneath. This post explains which component answers each question, where to scrape it, and the metric renames that can break an otherwise valid alert query.

The short answer​

ComponentMeasuresWhere it gets the dataMetric prefixUse it for
kube-state-metricsThe state of Kubernetes objects: desired vs actual replicas, pod phase, container restarts, resource requests and limitsWatches the API serverkube_Alerting and dashboards
cAdvisorWhat each container actually uses: CPU, memory, throttling, filesystem, networkBuilt into the kubelet, served at /metrics/cadvisorcontainer_Alerting and dashboards
node_exporterThe machine underneath: CPU modes, memory, disks, filesystems, network interfacesA DaemonSet reading /proc and /sys on each nodenode_Alerting and dashboards
metrics-serverA CPU and memory snapshot for each pod and nodeScrapes the kubelet's /metrics/resourcenone; it serves the Metrics API (metrics.k8s.io)kubectl top, the Horizontal and Vertical Pod Autoscalers

You will also meet two more sources. The kubelet's own /metrics endpoint provides things like kubelet_volume_stats_available_bytes, which tells you how full a PersistentVolume is. The API server exposes apiserver_* metrics about itself. Neither belongs to the four above, and alert rules use both.

Do you need kube-state-metrics, metrics-server or both?​

Choose by the consumer of the data:

  • HPA based on Pod CPU or memory, or kubectl top: metrics-server provides the Resource Metrics API for this path. kube-state-metrics does not replace it. An HPA based on custom or external metrics can use a different adapter.
  • Alerts about desired state: use kube-state-metrics for unavailable Deployment replicas, failed Jobs, restart counts and Pod waiting reasons. Scrape its /metrics endpoint into Prometheus or a compatible store.
  • Container CPU and memory dashboards or alerts: scrape the kubelet's container resource metrics, commonly /metrics/cadvisor, into the monitoring store. kube-state-metrics supplies requests and limits to compare the usage with.
  • Host disk, network and operating-system checks: use node_exporter on each node.

In a cluster that uses CPU-based autoscaling and Prometheus alerting, these are complementary data paths. You do not have to route metrics-server through Prometheus, or install kube-state-metrics just to make kubectl top work. The kube-state-metrics README and Kubernetes resource metrics pipeline explain the distinction.

kube-state-metrics: what the API server believes​

kube-state-metrics listens to the API server and turns objects into metrics. Its README calls this "the health of the various objects inside" the cluster, as opposed to the health of the cluster components themselves. It exposes the values as the API returns them. It does not apply the heuristics kubectl uses, which is why its numbers sometimes differ from what kubectl get prints.

That makes it the right source for questions about intent:

  • Does the Deployment have the replicas it asked for? kube_deployment_spec_replicas vs kube_deployment_status_replicas_available.
  • Is a container stuck in CrashLoopBackOff? kube_pod_container_status_waiting_reason.
  • Why did the last run end? kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason, where reason="OOMKilled" is the one you usually want.
  • Is a node NotReady? kube_node_status_condition.

It tells you nothing about usage. A pod at 100% of its CPU limit and an idle pod look the same to kube-state-metrics. For usage you need cAdvisor.

The rename that breaks old queries. kube-state-metrics 2.0 removed the per-resource metrics such as kube_pod_container_resource_limits_cpu_cores and kube_pod_container_resource_requests_memory_bytes. Their replacements are kube_pod_container_resource_limits and kube_pod_container_resource_requests, with resource and unit labels:

# kube-state-metrics 1.x (removed in 2.0)
kube_pod_container_resource_limits_cpu_cores

# kube-state-metrics 2.x
kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="cpu", unit="core"}

A query that uses the old name does not fail. It returns an empty result, and an alert rule built on it never fires. We found exactly this in our own Kubernetes template while writing this post: the container CPU rule still used the 1.x metric name and the old pod_name label. It now uses the current names.

cAdvisor: what containers actually use​

cAdvisor is compiled into the kubelet, so there is nothing extra to deploy. Prometheus scrapes it from each node at /metrics/cadvisor. These are the metrics you reach for when a pod is slow or keeps getting killed:

  • container_cpu_usage_seconds_total: CPU time consumed. Take a rate() to get cores in use.
  • container_memory_working_set_bytes: the container's working-set estimate. It is not the same as RSS or a definitive measurement of unreclaimable memory; active file cache can contribute to it. Use the termination reason as well when diagnosing an OOM kill.
  • container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total and container_cpu_cfs_periods_total: how often the container hit its CPU limit and was paused. The CPUThrottlingHigh rule is the ratio of the two.

Two things trip people up:

  1. Extra series. cAdvisor also reports cgroups that are not your application container: a pod-level series with container="" and, on older Docker-based nodes, the pause container as container="POD". Summing without a filter counts the same memory twice. Add container!="" (and container!="POD" on old nodes) when you aggregate.
  2. Label names changed. Older Kubernetes examples use pod_name and container_name. Current kubelet metrics use pod and container. Grouping by a missing pod_name label loses the intended Pod identity; joins that expect the old labels can return no matches or combine the wrong series. Check the labels on the data you actually scrape.

Usage becomes useful when you compare it with a limit, and the limit lives in kube-state-metrics. Both sides share the namespace, pod and container labels, so the join is direct:

max by (cluster, namespace, pod, container) (
  container_memory_working_set_bytes{container!="", container!="POD"}
)
/
(
  max by (cluster, namespace, pod, container) (
    kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="memory", unit="byte"}
  ) > 0
)
> 0.9

Both sides must identify the same container. Preserve a common cluster label when querying multiple clusters; adapt the grouping labels to your setup. The positive-limit filter excludes containers without a positive memory limit, and max avoids adding identical duplicate scrape series together. This is a threshold against configured limits, not proof that the workload is about to be OOM-killed. The cAdvisor metric reference describes the usage metrics.

node_exporter: the machine underneath​

On Kubernetes, node_exporter commonly runs as a DaemonSet with access to the host's /proc and /sys. It knows nothing about pods. It reports the operating system: node_cpu_seconds_total by mode, node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes, node_filesystem_avail_bytes, disk I/O and network errors.

Use it for the questions Kubernetes does not answer. Is the node's root filesystem filling up? Is the clock drifting? Is a NIC dropping packets? Is the kernel OOM killer firing (node_vmstat_oom_kill)? Node-level memory includes page cache and every process on the host, so it will not add up to the sum of your containers. That is expected.

The Linux rule set covers the common host checks, including disk-fill prediction with predict_linear.

metrics-server: the autoscaling data path​

metrics-server collects CPU and memory every 15 seconds from each kubelet's /metrics/resource endpoint and serves them through the Metrics API. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler reads it, the Vertical Pod Autoscaler reads it, and kubectl top reads it.

It keeps recent resource values in memory rather than a queryable monitoring history. Its own /metrics endpoint exposes self-monitoring, not a replacement Prometheus feed for every Pod's CPU and memory. The project's README says metrics-server is intended for autoscaling rather than forwarding metrics to monitoring solutions. If you want resource data in a monitoring store, scrape the appropriate kubelet endpoints directly.

So when kubectl top and a dashboard disagree, check the sampling window, aggregation, endpoint and metric definition before assuming either value is wrong. For the endpoint layout, see the Kubernetes system metrics guide.

Can metrics-server replace Prometheus?​

metrics-server serves the resource API used by autoscaling and kubectl top. Prometheus scrapes and stores time series for historical queries and rule evaluation. Installing one does not provide the other one's consumer APIs or operating model.

If you are choosing where the alert rules themselves should run, Grafana Alerting vs Alertmanager compares evaluation and notification ownership. The metric sources in this article can remain the same whichever evaluation path you choose.

Which component answers your question​

QuestionMetricSource
Is the pod restarting?kube_pod_container_status_restarts_totalkube-state-metrics
Was it OOM-killed?kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason{reason="OOMKilled"}kube-state-metrics
Is a container close to its memory limit?container_memory_working_set_bytes ÷ kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="memory"}cAdvisor + kube-state-metrics
Is it being CPU-throttled?container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total ÷ container_cpu_cfs_periods_totalcAdvisor
Does the Deployment have the replicas it wants?kube_deployment_status_replicas_available vs kube_deployment_spec_replicaskube-state-metrics
Is a node NotReady?kube_node_status_condition{condition="Ready"}kube-state-metrics
Is a node's disk filling up?node_filesystem_avail_bytesnode_exporter
Is a PersistentVolume filling up?kubelet_volume_stats_available_byteskubelet
How much CPU is the pod using right now?kubectl top podmetrics-server

Ready-made rules, sorted by source​

Most of the standard Kubernetes alerts read kube-state-metrics. Each of these pages explains what the alert means, its common causes and the steps to fix it, and lists the metrics it uses:

  • kube-state-metrics: KubePodCrashLooping, KubePodNotReady, KubeDeploymentReplicasMismatch, KubeNodeNotReady, KubeJobFailed, KubeHpaMaxedOut
  • kubelet: KubePersistentVolumeFillingUp
  • cAdvisor: CPUThrottlingHigh
  • API server: KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn, KubeClientCertificateExpiration

The full Kubernetes rule set is available as a Prometheus rules file you can download and load with rule_files.

With Nightingale​

Nightingale does not replace any of these four components. It queries the store where their metrics already land, such as Prometheus or VictoriaMetrics, and runs alert rules against it. The Kubernetes integration ships the rules above, each with its runbook attached, and you can import them into a business group in one step.

item.title: MCP server for alerting: six design decisions
item.description: How Nightingale's built-in MCP server handles permissions, write access and audit: RBAC inherited from the token, write tools unregistered by default, no delete tools, and one caveat.
item.content:encoded:
Since v9, the Nightingale process is also an MCP server. Claude Code, Cursor or any other MCP client can connect to /mcp and ask which alerts are firing, which rules are noisiest, or what a metric did over the last hour.

The tool list was the easy part. The hard questions were about trust. Whose permissions does the AI client have? What can it change? How do you find out afterwards what it did? This post walks through the six decisions we made, and one caveat we haven't solved.

What this is not: an autonomous agent that resolves incidents on its own. It is a way for a model to read, and with explicit opt-in to change, an alerting system with the same permissions as the person who connected it.

1. No separate server: the endpoint lives in the process​

There is nothing extra to deploy. POST /mcp is served by the same n9e process that serves the UI and the API, and it is on by default.

It uses MCP's Streamable HTTP transport in stateless mode. Every POST is self-contained. The server returns an Mcp-Session-Id on initialize but never validates it, and GET /mcp returns 405 because there is no standalone event stream. The practical benefit: several Nightingale instances behind a load balancer need no sticky sessions. Any instance can answer any request.

2. A tool call is an internal API call​

When a client calls list_alert_rules, the MCP server does not read the database. It dispatches the call, in-process, onto Nightingale's own HTTP route (/api/n9e/busi-group/{gid}/alert-rules), carrying the caller's token through the full middleware chain: authenticate, resolve the user, check the permission point, check the business group.

So the answer to "can the AI get around RBAC?" is structural: no. It walks the same path as a click in the UI. There is no separate permission model for AI to configure, audit and keep in sync.

The consequence is that a client has exactly the permissions of its token's owner. To limit what the AI can see, you give it a limited account: a dedicated user with the Guest or Standard role, in a team that can read only the business groups you choose. list_busi_groups returns only groups that user can reach, so the model can only ever pick from that set. Do not give the AI account the Admin role. Admin bypasses the business-group layer.

OAuth tokens get one more restriction. A token issued through OAuth works on /mcp and /a2a only; the rest of the API rejects it.

3. Write tools are not registered, not just refused​

There are 74 tools. 42 read and 32 write. By default only the 42 read tools exist. The write tools sit in a separate registration list that is skipped unless you set:

[HTTP.A2A]
MCPEnableWriteTools = true

We chose "not registered" over "registered and refused" on purpose. A model plans with the tools it can see. If write tools appear in tools/list and fail at call time, the model keeps trying them, or tries to work around the error. If they are absent, the model never considers them.

This gate sits outside RBAC. Even if a client is handed root's token by mistake, under the default config it cannot change anything. Every tool also carries MCP's readOnlyHint annotation for clients that use it, and it always agrees with the registration list.

4. No delete tools at all​

None of the 74 tools deletes anything. "Write" means create and update. Deleting a rule, a user or a business group is not reachable through MCP.

This changes the worst case from "gone" to "changed wrongly", which is easier to notice and to fix. It does not make write tools harmless. Some of them are among the most powerful operations in the product:

ToolWhy it is dangerous
reset_user_passwordResets any user's password
create_user, update_user_profileAssign roles as a side effect, which is privilege escalation
bind_role_operationsReplaces a role's whole permission set; a short payload silently removes permissions
create_notify_channel, update_notify_channelA webhook channel sends alert content to any address it is given
upsert_datasourceStores data source credentials and probes the address it is given
set_dashboard_publicMakes a dashboard readable without login
toggle_alert_rules, set_datasource_status, create_muteCreate blind spots: rules disabled, a data source off, alerts silenced

5. Toolsets are an allowlist, and typos don't fall back​

The 74 tools are grouped into 13 toolsets: alerts, targets, datasource, mutes, busi_groups, notify_rules, alert_subscribes, event_pipelines, users, metrics, logs, dashboards and roles. An empty list exposes all of them; a list exposes only those named:

[HTTP.A2A]
MCPToolsets = ["alerts", "busi_groups", "targets", "metrics"]

A misspelled name is dropped with a warning in the log. It does not fall back to "everything". A list made entirely of typos exposes zero tools, not 74. Failing closed is less convenient and much safer.

Work backwards from what you want the AI to do:

UseToolsets
On-call triage: what is firing, which rule, who owns italerts, busi_groups, targets
Plus "explain this spike"add metrics
Noise review: noisiest rules, mutes, subscriptionsadd mutes, alert_subscribes
Letting the AI change configurationturn on writes, and remove users and roles first

6. Every call is attributable​

Two trails answer "who changed this, and was it the AI?":

  • The object itself. A rule, mute or dashboard changed over MCP records the token owner's username in update_by, exactly as if they had edited it in the UI.

  • The request log. Every /mcp request writes a start line with the full request body (tool name and arguments) and a done line with the user and status code, joined by a trace_id:

    grep '"method":"tools/call"' n9e.log | grep -oE '"name":"[a-z_]+"' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

    Oversized bodies are truncated, and the log line says so.

A dedicated account per client makes both trails useful. If every client shares one token, update_by tells you nothing.

The caveat: query_logs and SQL data sources​

One read-only tool deserves care. query_logs in the logs toolset passes the query body to Nightingale's log query endpoint, which dispatches on the data source type. If you have SQL data sources registered (MySQL, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, Doris or TDengine), the SQL runs as written.

There is a read-only check on that path. It is a keyword blocklist that rejects statements containing INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP, ALTER, CREATE, TRUNCATE, REPLACE, GRANT or REVOKE. That stops the obvious cases. It is not a SQL parser, so treat it as a second line of defence rather than a guarantee. If you have SQL data sources, leave logs out of MCPToolsets, or give the AI account a role that cannot reach those data sources. Registering them with read-only database credentials is a sensible extra layer.

MCP or the built-in assistant?​

Nightingale also has a built-in assistant in the UI. For configuration changes it is the safer of the two: its update operations are two-phase. The first call computes the change and shows a confirmation card, and nothing is written until a person confirms. MCP has no such step. A write tool writes on its first call.

So a reasonable split is: use an MCP client for reading and triage, where its own model and tools shine, and use the built-in assistant when something needs to change.

Try it​

Create a token for a dedicated, least-privileged user under Profile → Token management, then add Nightingale to your MCP client:

~/.claude.json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "nightingale": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://127.0.0.1:17000/mcp",
      "headers": { "X-User-Token": "<token of the AI account>" }
    }
  }
}

Then ask something you can check: "Which alerts are firing right now? Group them by severity." or "List every business group I can see." The second one is also a quick test that the account is scoped the way you intended.

More detail is in the docs: Enable the MCP endpoint, Permission inheritance and RBAC, Read and write toolsets and Enable write tools safely.

item.title: Prometheus high availability: storage vs alerting
item.description: Running two Prometheus replicas solves half of high availability. How Alertmanager clustering, replica labels and Thanos, Mimir or VictoriaMetrics deduplication fit together.
item.content:encoded:
Ask how to make Prometheus highly available and the usual answer is "run two of them". That is correct, and it is only half the job. Two replicas give you two copies of every alert and two slightly different copies of every time series. Each needs its own fix, and the fixes don't share a configuration.

This post separates the two problems: keeping alerts flowing exactly once, and keeping the data queryable without gaps. It ends with a checklist.

How Prometheus does HA​

Prometheus has no clustering. High availability means running two (or more) identical servers. Each one scrapes the same targets, evaluates the same rules and keeps its own local copy of the data. They don't talk to each other.

The copies are never identical. Each replica scrapes at its own moment, so the timestamps differ. When one replica restarts, it has a gap that the other doesn't. That is fine for alerting, and a problem for dashboards.

The usual convention is to give each replica an external label that says which one it is:

# prometheus-a.yml (prometheus-b.yml says replica: b)
global:
  external_labels:
    cluster: prod-eu
    replica: a

Problem 1: alerts should arrive once, even when a replica dies​

Both replicas evaluate every rule, so both send every alert. Deduplication happens in Alertmanager.

Cluster the Alertmanagers. Alertmanager instances gossip with each other. You start each one with --cluster.peer pointing at the others, and they share notification state and silences. When two replicas send the same alert, the cluster sends one notification.

Point every Prometheus at every Alertmanager. The Alertmanager README is explicit: do not load-balance traffic between Prometheus and its Alertmanagers. Give each Prometheus the full list, because every alert has to reach every instance:

alerting:
  alertmanagers:
    - static_configs:
        - targets: ['am-0:9093', 'am-1:9093', 'am-2:9093']

Drop the replica label from alerts. Alerts carry the external labels. If replica A sends {alertname="X", replica="a"} and replica B sends {alertname="X", replica="b"}, Alertmanager sees two different alerts and notifies twice. Strip the label on the way out:

alerting:
  alert_relabel_configs:
    - action: labeldrop
      regex: replica

The Prometheus Operator does this for you with its own replica label. Hand-built setups often miss it, and the symptom is that every page arrives twice.

With these three in place, alerting HA works well. If replica A dies, replica B was evaluating the same rules all along, so there is no gap in detection. If an Alertmanager dies, Prometheus is still sending to the others.

Problem 2: dashboards and queries should not show gaps​

This is the half that "run two" does not solve. Point Grafana at replica A, and you see replica A's gaps. Put a load balancer in front of both, and consecutive refreshes can hit different replicas and draw slightly different lines.

The fix is a layer that knows the two replicas hold the same data and merges them. The three common options handle the replica label in different ways, and that difference matters:

StoreHow it deduplicatesWhat the replicas' labels must look like
ThanosThanos Querier merges series that differ only in the label named by --query.replica-labelDifferent: each replica has its own replica value
Grafana MimirThe HA tracker elects a leader replica per cluster, keeps its samples and drops the rest. It switches leader if the current one sends nothing for 30 seconds by defaultDifferent: cluster plus a __replica__ label by default
VictoriaMetrics-dedup.minScrapeInterval keeps one sample per series per interval. Set it equal to your scrape_intervalIdentical: the docs require the HA pair to write the same series, so no per-replica label

So a setup moved from Thanos to VictoriaMetrics needs its replica label removed, and a setup moved the other way needs one added. Mixing the conventions gives you either doubled series or a store that silently keeps one replica.

Long-term retention is a separate decision from HA. Thanos, Mimir and VictoriaMetrics also keep data longer than a local Prometheus. But you can have deduplicated HA with short retention, or long retention with a single replica. Decide each one on its own.

Scaling is not HA​

Federation, functional sharding (one Prometheus per team or per cluster) and hashmod sharding spread load. They don't add redundancy: each shard is still a single point of failure until you run it as a pair. If you shard, every shard needs the replica treatment above.

Where a separate alerting engine changes the picture​

The Grafana Alerting vs Alertmanager guide explains rule ownership and how the two can share an external notification path.

Everything above assumes Prometheus evaluates the rules. Some setups move evaluation out of Prometheus: Grafana Alerting, vmalert, Thanos Ruler, or Nightingale. Then storage HA and alerting HA become two different systems.

Nightingale takes a different approach from a Prometheus pair, with a different trade-off:

  • It queries one deduplicated data source. Prometheus behind Thanos Querier, VictoriaMetrics or Mimir. The storage-side HA from Problem 2 is still needed, and Nightingale doesn't replace it.
  • Rules are shared out, not duplicated. Several n9e instances share one MySQL and one Redis. Each live instance sends a heartbeat every second. The live instances form a consistent hash ring per data source, and each rule runs on exactly one instance. One evaluation means one event, so no Alertmanager-style deduplication is needed.
  • The trade-off is a failover gap. An instance counts as dead after 30 seconds without a heartbeat, and only then does its share of rules move to another instance. A freshly started instance also waits 30 seconds before evaluating. A Prometheus pair has no such gap, because the other replica was evaluating all along.
  • Shared dependencies need their own HA. If MySQL is down, everything is down. If Redis is unreachable at startup, the process exits. Running several n9e instances protects against losing an n9e process, and nothing else.

Neither design is better in general. Duplicate evaluation with downstream deduplication gives zero-gap failover and costs you a deduplication layer that must be configured exactly right. Single evaluation with a hash ring avoids duplicates by construction and costs you up to 30 seconds of blindness for the rules on a failed instance. The details are in High availability and failure domains.

Checklist​

Alerting

  • Two or more Prometheus replicas with identical rule files.
  • Alertmanager clustered with --cluster.peer; the cluster port reachable between instances.
  • Every Prometheus lists every Alertmanager. No load balancer in between.
  • The replica label dropped in alert_relabel_configs.
  • Tested: stop one replica and one Alertmanager, fire a test alert, and get exactly one notification.

Storage and queries

  • A deduplicating layer: Thanos Querier, Mimir's HA tracker or VictoriaMetrics deduplication.
  • Replica labels set the way that layer expects. Thanos and Mimir need them to differ; VictoriaMetrics needs them identical.
  • Dashboards and alert rules query the deduplicated endpoint, not a single replica.
  • Tested: restart one replica and check that a dashboard over that window shows no gap.

Everything

  • The monitoring system is monitored from outside itself. A dead-man's-switch alert that always fires, and pages when it stops arriving, catches the case where the whole alerting path is down.

The last item is the one most often skipped. Every check above runs inside the system it is checking.

item.title: Symptom-based alerting with Prometheus
item.description: Symptom-based vs cause-based alerting with real Prometheus rules: error ratio, latency and probe alerts that page, and where CPU, disk and certificate alerts still belong.
item.content:encoded:
At 3 a.m. an alert says CPU is at 92% on db-3. The on-call engineer opens the dashboards. Checkout is fast, errors are flat, and nobody is affected. The alert was true and useless.

A week later, checkout fails for 20 minutes because a dependency returns errors. CPU is fine, memory is fine, every host looks healthy. No alert fires.

Both failures have the same root cause: the rules watch causes, not symptoms. This post explains the difference, shows what symptom rules look like in PromQL, and explains where cause alerts still earn their place.

Symptoms and causes​

A symptom is what users experience: requests failing, pages loading slowly, a service unreachable, data arriving late. A cause is why: a saturated CPU, a full disk, a crashed pod, a slow query.

The idea comes from Google's SRE book. Chapter 6, "Monitoring Distributed Systems", argues that paging should be driven by symptoms, and proposes four golden signals to watch on every user-facing system: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Rob Ewaschuk's essay "My Philosophy on Alerting", written while he was an SRE at Google, makes the same case in more detail.

Cause-based paging fails in two directions:

  • Causes without symptoms create noise. High CPU, a pod restart, one replica out of three down. Systems absorb these all the time. Each page that turns out to be harmless teaches people to ignore the next one.
  • Symptoms without a known cause create silence. You can only write cause rules for failures you have imagined. A new failure mode, a dependency outage or a bad deploy that leaves every resource metric normal goes unnoticed.

A symptom rule catches both the failures you predicted and the ones you didn't, because it watches the outcome instead of the mechanism.

What symptom rules look like​

The metric names below follow common conventions. Yours will depend on your instrumentation library, ingress controller or service mesh.

Errors: the share of requests that fail.

sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout", code=~"5.."}[5m]))
  /
sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[5m]))
> 0.02

Use a ratio, not a count. 50 errors a minute is a disaster at 100 requests and noise at 100,000.

Latency: how slow the slow requests are.

histogram_quantile(0.99,
  sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="checkout"}[5m]))
) > 1

Alert on a high percentile, not the average. An average of 200 ms can hide one request in fifty taking ten seconds.

Availability from outside. A probe that calls the service the way a user would catches DNS, TLS, load balancer and network failures that internal metrics never see. With the Prometheus blackbox exporter that is probe_success == 0. Our Linux rule set includes an "HTTP probe failed" rule for Categraf's HTTP checks.

Freshness and throughput for things that are not request-driven. Did the nightly job run? Is the queue draining?

time() - batch_job_last_success_timestamp_seconds{job="nightly-export"} > 26 * 3600

Three details that make symptom rules work​

  1. Measure where users are. The ingress or load balancer sees every request, including the ones that never reached a healthy pod. Per-pod error rates miss requests that were dropped before reaching any pod.

  2. Aggregate across instances. sum(...) over the whole service, not one alert per pod. Users don't care which replica failed them.

  3. Guard against low traffic. At three requests a minute, one failure is a 33% error ratio. Add a minimum volume:

    (
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout", code=~"5.."}[5m]))
        / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[5m]))
    ) > 0.02
    and
    sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[5m])) > 1

Where cause alerts still belong​

"Alert on symptoms" doesn't mean "delete every cause alert". Some causes deserve a notification. They just shouldn't wake anyone up.

Deadlines. A disk that will be full in 24 hours, or a certificate that expires in 7 days, is a symptom waiting to happen, with a known date. Alert on these during working hours, at warning severity. The Linux library has a predict_linear rule for disks; the Kubernetes library has certificate expiry rules.

Lost redundancy. One replica of three is down. Users are fine, but the next failure will hurt them. That is worth a ticket today, not a page tonight.

The monitoring itself. If a scrape target or collector stops reporting, every rule that depends on it looks healthy. up == 0, or a dead-man's-switch alert that always fires, is a cause alert you need from day one.

Explanation. Everything else, such as CPU, memory, GC pauses and connection counts, belongs on a dashboard or as a low-severity alert that someone looks at while investigating a symptom. The Kubernetes rules in our library follow this: "Node CPU usage exceeds 90%" ships at info severity, while the symptom-shaped rules such as KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn go up to critical.

Connecting symptoms to causes​

A symptom alert tells you that something is wrong. The responder then needs to know where to look. Two ways to close that gap:

  • Put the causes in the runbook. Every symptom alert should link to a list of likely causes and the commands that confirm each one. Each page in our alert rule library follows that shape: what the alert means, common causes, then the steps to fix it. KubePodCrashLooping is a typical example.
  • Mute symptoms while a known cause is active. If a whole site loses its uplink, every service there reports errors. Alertmanager's inhibit_rules, or an equivalent, can mute the dependent alerts while the upstream alert is firing. That needs a shared label such as site on both.

A worked example​

Here is a rule set for a checkout service built on these ideas:

RuleKindSeverityWho hears about it
Error ratio above 2% for 5 minutesSymptomCriticalPage
p99 latency above 1 s for 10 minutesSymptomCriticalPage
External probe failing from 2 or more locationsSymptomCriticalPage
Error ratio above 0.5% for 30 minutesSymptom, slow burnWarningTeam channel
Disk full within 24 hoursCause with a deadlineWarningTeam channel
One of three replicas down for 15 minutesLost redundancyWarningTeam channel
Scrape target downMonitoringWarningTeam channel
CPU, memory, GC, DB connectionsCauseInfo or dashboardNobody, until someone investigates

Three rules can page, and all three describe something a customer would notice.

Auditing a rule set you already have​

For each rule that can page, ask: if this fires and users are fine, would anyone do anything? If the answer is no, lower its severity or move it to a dashboard.

Then look at the data. List the rules that fired most often in the last month and how many of those firings led to an action. Also list the rules that never fired in a year. They are usually broken rather than lucky: a renamed metric, a label that changed, a threshold that cannot be reached. Nightingale's built-in assistant can answer both questions directly ("which rules fired most often in the last 7 days, and which have never fired?"); see Common investigation workflows.

For the rules that stay, the rule design best practices page covers naming, labels and how much one rule should cover.

item.title: Migrating from Zabbix to Prometheus
item.description: A concept-by-concept map from Zabbix to Prometheus: hosts, items, triggers, LLD, dependencies, maintenance. Plus the gaps with no equivalent and a migration order that never turns Zabbix off.
item.content:encoded:
Moving from Zabbix to Prometheus is not a data migration. There is no export file that turns into rule files, and no tool that converts triggers into PromQL. The two systems model monitoring differently. Most of the work is translating concepts, then rebuilding a smaller set of rules on top of them.

This post maps each Zabbix concept to its Prometheus counterpart, lists the parts that have no equivalent, and suggests an order of work that keeps Zabbix running until the end.

The difference that explains everything else​

Zabbix is host-centric. You create a host, attach templates, and the templates define items (what to collect) and triggers (when to alert) for that host. 40 database servers with one template give you 40 copies of each trigger.

Prometheus is query-centric. Exporters expose metrics, Prometheus scrapes them, and an alert rule is a query. A rule matches every series the query returns. One rule covers all 40 servers, and the 41st server is covered as soon as it is scraped.

Most of the translation follows from this. You rarely port triggers one by one; you merge them.

Concept map​

Collection and storage​

ZabbixPrometheusNotes
Zabbix server and databasePrometheus server and its local TSDBLocal retention is short by default (15 days). Long-term storage is a separate component
Zabbix agentExporters: node_exporter for hosts, mysqld_exporter for MySQL and so onPrometheus pulls over HTTP; the agent's active checks push. Targets must be reachable from Prometheus
Zabbix proxyA Prometheus server per site, or Prometheus in agent mode with remote_writeAgent mode scrapes and forwards without evaluating rules locally
ItemA metric name plus labelsWhich metrics exist is decided by the exporter, not by the monitoring server
Item key vfs.fs.size[/,pfree]node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/"} ÷ node_filesystem_size_bytes{mountpoint="/"}Percentages are usually computed in the query
Calculated itemRecording rule
History and trendsRaw samples; downsampling only in long-term stores such as ThanosThere is no built-in hourly min/avg/max like Zabbix trends
Text and log itemsNonePrometheus stores numbers only. Logs go to Loki, Elasticsearch or similar

Hosts, templates and discovery​

ZabbixPrometheusNotes
HostA scrape target, identified by the instance label
Host groupLabels such as team or env, added through relabelingGroups become labels you can filter on
TemplateAn exporter, a rule file and a dashboardThe community equivalent of a template collection is a monitoring mixin
Low-level discovery (LLD)Service discovery for targets; labels for things on a targetNew filesystems or interfaces appear as new series automatically. No discovery rule needed
User macros {$THRESHOLD}Hard-coded thresholds, or a threshold metric joined in the queryPer-host overrides need a pattern, see below

Triggers and alerting​

ZabbixPrometheusNotes
TriggerAlerting rule: a PromQL expr plus forOne rule, many series
Trigger severity (six levels)A severity labelA convention, not a built-in. Most teams use three: critical, warning, info
Recovery expression, hysteresisNo direct equivalentkeep_firing_for delays recovery; true hysteresis needs a query trick
nodata()absent(), absent_over_time(), or up == 0absent() only works for series you name explicitly
Trigger dependenciesAlertmanager inhibit_rulesInhibition mutes target alerts while a source alert fires, matched on labels
Event correlationNone in Prometheus or Alertmanager

Notification​

ZabbixPrometheusNotes
Action and operationsAlertmanager routes and receiversRouting matches on labels
Media typeReceiver integration: email, Slack, webhook and others
Escalation stepsNot built inAlertmanager repeats notifications (repeat_interval) but has no escalation chain. That is an on-call tool's job
Maintenance periodSilences, plus mute_time_intervals for recurring windowsSilences are ad hoc; time intervals cover the weekly window
AcknowledgementNone in AlertmanagerUsually handled in the on-call or chat tool

The parts with no equivalent​

Plan for these before you start. They are where migrations stall.

  1. Escalations. Zabbix can notify the on-call engineer, then the team lead after 30 minutes, then the manager. Alertmanager cannot. If you rely on escalation, you need an on-call tool behind Alertmanager.

  2. Per-host thresholds. In Zabbix you override {$DISK_PFREE_MIN} on one host. In Prometheus a threshold is part of the query. The common workaround is a small metric that carries thresholds, joined in the rule:

    (node_filesystem_avail_bytes / node_filesystem_size_bytes) * 100
      < on(instance) group_left()
    disk_free_threshold_percent

    Or keep a default rule and split the exceptions out by label: disk_profile="large" gets its own rule.

  3. SNMP traps. The SNMP exporter polls; it does not receive traps. Traps need a separate receiver that turns them into metrics or logs.

  4. Text and log items. If Zabbix watches log files or string values, those move to a log system, not Prometheus.

  5. Trigger dependencies, partly. inhibit_rules cover the common case of "switch down mutes everything behind it". They need a label that links the two alerts, such as a shared site or rack. Zabbix's dependency tree has no labels to rely on, so you add them first.

An order that keeps Zabbix running​

Zabbix stays up and keeps paging people until the very last step. Each step can be checked on its own.

  1. Deploy exporters next to the Zabbix agents. Start with one group of hosts. Leave the agents installed. Check: the targets are up in Prometheus.
  2. Pick the storage you will keep. A single Prometheus for a start; a pair and a long-term store if you need HA or longer retention. Decide now, because changing stores later is a project of its own.
  3. Import existing rule sets instead of porting templates. The community rules for node_exporter, MySQL, Redis, Kubernetes and others cover most of what stock Zabbix templates do. Our alert rule library has them as downloadable rule files, each with a runbook.
  4. Port the custom triggers, merged. List your custom triggers, group them by item and threshold, and write one rule per group. Use labels for the exceptions.
  5. Send Prometheus alerts somewhere nobody is paged. A dedicated channel or mailbox. Compare it with Zabbix every day: fired only in Zabbix (missed rule or metric), fired only in Prometheus (threshold typo, or a Zabbix dependency or maintenance window you forgot), fired in both at different severity.
  6. Move notification one channel at a time. Chat first, then email, then phone. Disable the matching Zabbix action as each channel moves, but keep Zabbix evaluating so the daily comparison continues.
  7. Stop Zabbix last. After a week with no differences, stop the agents. Keep the database read-only for as long as you need the history. History does not migrate.

Zabbix or Prometheus at all?​

Not every Zabbix setup should move. Zabbix suits fleets of long-lived hosts and network devices, teams that want everything configured in one UI, and environments that need agents to push through firewalls. Prometheus suits environments where targets come and go (containers, autoscaling), where configuration lives in Git, and where software already exposes /metrics. Many organisations run both for years: Zabbix for network gear and legacy hosts, Prometheus for Kubernetes and new services.
